*Reading the Rocks: Rapid Continental Separation, Animal Diversification, Arctic Megafauna Burial, and Human Lifespan Decline After the Global Flood*

Following Noah’s global Flood approximately 3300 BC, a single supercontinent persisted for several centuries until a large asteroid impact between 2800 and 2900 BC, during the days of Peleg around 530 years after the Flood, triggered Catastrophic Plate Movement. This event caused rapid continental separation, isolating animal kinds and driving their diversification. 

The catastrophe also generated massive tsunamis that led to flash flooding and the instantaneous freezing of Arctic megafauna. Human lifespans, already shortened after the Flood, declined sharply again after the impact due to environmental and genetic stressors. Supporting evidence includes young ocean crust, thin deep-sea sediments, matching fossils across continents, Burckle Crater, chevron dunes, and exquisitely preserved Arctic animal remains.
 The Genesis account describes a global Flood that destroyed and reshaped Earth’s surface. Using the Septuagint chronology, the Flood occurred roughly 1400 years earlier than in the Masoretic Text, allowing approximately 530 years from the Flood to Peleg’s birth. Genesis 10:25 states that “in his days the earth was divided,” literally a catastrophic physical separation of the continents as well as the isolation and consolidation of family groups which began speaking their own languages. 

This paper integrates rapid post-Flood continental breakup, diversification within created kinds, sudden Arctic animal burial, and human lifespan decline—all within a known historical framework.

Glacial striations on South America, Africa, India, and Australia indicate significant ice buildup over a southern polar region. Northern areas remained temperate, supporting diverse megafauna.
 Around 530 years after the Flood, in the days of Peleg, a large asteroid struck the Indian Ocean, forming Burckle Crater. This impact fractured the supercontinent and initiated plate movement assisted by the earth’s centrifugal force. Mega-tsunamis radiated outward, evidenced by enormous chevron dunes in Madagascar and Australia.

In the centuries following the global Flood, the post-Flood Earth became geologically unstable beneath the single supercontinent. The growing weight of southern polar ice became unstable and the partial hardening of the sediments weakened the crust and mantle. This instability culminated in catastrophe when the asteroid struck. The impact not only triggered rapid continental separation via Catastrophic Plate Tectonics but also caused major climatic shifts.

*Rapid Continental Separation and Geological Catastrophes* The continents moved rapidly apart and moved north over a relatively short period, rebalancing Earth’s landmass northward. This movement accounts for matching dinosaur tracks between Brazil and Cameroon on Flood-deposited sediments, the formation of young oceanic crust, the formation of mountain ranges, the Mid Atlantic Ridge and the Marianas Trench. The shift and movement of the plates also generated massive tsunamis as the continents surged into the Arctic region.
 As the continents separated, animal populations were isolated, continuing diversification within their original created kinds. Examples include:

• Ursids (bears) → brown bears and grizzly bears (Eurasia/North America), American black bears (North America), polar bears (Arctic), and Asian black bears and sloth bears (Asia) 
• Felids → lions, tigers, leopards, jaguars, and saber-toothed cats (Smilodon in the Americas; Homotherium across Eurasia including Siberia)

• Otters → river otters, sea otters, and giant otters across multiple continents 
• Tapirs→ tapirs in South America and Southeast Asia 
• Marsupials → opossums/possums in the Americas (three different kinds) and Asia

• Sciurids→ tree squirrels, ground squirrels, chipmunks, marmots, and flying squirrels distributed across continents

• Rabbits, Hares and other rodents across the globe  
• Pythons and crocodiles distributed across multiple continents

A striking example of relict biogeography tied to continental breakup is the monito del monte (Dromiciops gliroides) of southern South America.  It’s a *third* marsupial kind in South America. As the last representative of a hibernating Microbiotheria, it shares a closer phylogenetic relationship with *Australian* marsupials than with other Neotropical opossums and shrew like marsupials of South America. This distribution pattern aligns with rapid post-Flood plate tectonics and continental reconfiguration. The monito del monte exemplifies how isolated populations could persist in temperate forest refugia following major geophysical upheavals, while related lineages dispersed or adapted elsewhere.

This continental breakup model explains the presence of similar animals on now-separated continents without requiring millions of years or floating vegetation mats.
 The Genesis genealogies (using the Septuagint) show a clear pattern of declining human lifespans tied to the two major catastrophes:

Patriarchs routinely lived 700–969 years (e.g., Methuselah 969 years).

This “halving twice” pattern aligns with the environmental upheavals: atmospheric changes, increased cosmic radiation, climate volatility, volcanic activity, and genetic bottlenecks.

*Instant Freezing and Burial of Arctic Megafauna by Tsunamis*

*Key evidence:* The impact and continental movement triggered enormous tsunamis that rapidly flooded and froze northern regions. Numerous animals were buried and preserved mid-activity, many with undigested plants still in their mouths and stomachs. 

Preserved megafauna include woolly mammoths, mastodons, woolly rhinos, steppe bison, horses, reindeer, musk oxen, saber-toothed cats (Smilodon in the Americas and Homotherium in Siberia and Eurasia), cave lions, short-faced bears, cave bears, cave hyenas, steppe wolves, Arctic ground squirrels, wolverines, saiga antelope, wild yaks, moose, and Arctic hares.

*Lasting Evidence and Implications* Key supporting features include young ocean crust, thin deep-sea sediments, matching fossils across continents, Burckle Crater ejecta, chevron dunes, and the spectacularly preserved Arctic animal graveyards. This framework demonstrates that catastrophic processes operating over centuries, rather than eons, can account for the geological and biological evidence we observe.
 The Septuagint’s longer post-Flood timeline provides sufficient time for glaciers to develop, animals to spread widely, and civilizations to emerge before the catastrophic division in Peleg’s days. The evidence explains continental separation, animal distribution patterns, rapid freezing of megafauna, and human lifespan decline—all within the known historical biblical record.
